title: The Opposable Mind: How Successful Leaders Win Through Integrative Thinking
license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, author, year and publisher (Harvard Business School Press, ISBN 9781422118924) matched on publishersweekly.com, a Wikipedia entry and library listings. The companion article “How Successful Leaders Think” (Harvard Business Review, June 2007, vol. 85, no. 6, starting p. 60) matched in secondary listings; no official HBR page for it appeared in results, so it is not given its own record.

summary: Martin, then dean of the University of Toronto’s Rotman School of Management, argues that many effective leaders share a habit of mind he calls integrative thinking: holding two opposing models in tension and constructing a new model that keeps elements of each and is superior to both, rather than accepting a trade-off. He develops the idea from work with business leaders and argues that it can be learned and practiced.
arguments: Effective leaders resist forced choices between opposing models and search for a creative resolution.
Integrative thinkers treat more factors as salient, accept nonlinear and multidirectional causal relationships, and keep the whole problem in view while working on its parts.
An integrative resolution is better than either opposing model, not a compromise between them.
The capacity can be developed through practice and teaching.
design: Practitioner argument drawn from the author’s interviews and teaching with business leaders; no controlled comparison.
strengths: A clear, memorable prompt for looking past binary choices, and a useful distinction between integration and compromise.
limitations: Built on successful leaders’ accounts of their own thinking, so it is exposed to survivorship and to retrospective storytelling. There is no controlled evidence that training integrative thinking improves decisions.
contested: Not tested experimentally as a causal claim; treat it as a practitioner heuristic rather than a research finding.
generalizability: Usable as a deliberation prompt in any setting where opposing models compete, including sport organizations. Claims about its effectiveness do not generalize because they have not been tested.
relevance: Gives you a vocabulary for refusing false trade-offs when behavioral, financial, legal and strategic considerations collide — while practicing the course’s habit of labelling practitioner ideas as such.

title: A Surgical Safety Checklist to Reduce Morbidity and Mortality in a Global Population
authors: et al. (Safe Surgery Saves Lives Study Group)
license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, first author, journal, volume, issue, pages, year (Epub 14 January 2009) and DOI matched on PubMed (PMID 19144931); sample sizes and headline rates matched in press summaries; a repository copy appeared on dash.harvard.edu. The full author list was not displayed in results, so only the first author and study group are recorded.

summary: A before-and-after study of a 19-item surgical safety checklist introduced in eight hospitals in eight cities with WHO collaboration. Comparing 3,733 patients before introduction with 3,955 after, the death rate fell from 1.5% to 0.8% and inpatient complications from 11.0% to 7.0%. The results helped make the checklist a global policy model.
arguments: A short, structured checklist used at defined points in an operation was followed by large reductions in deaths and complications.
Improvements appeared across hospitals in very different settings.
A simple process tool can change team behavior at critical moments.
design: Prospective before-and-after comparison in eight hospitals; no randomization and no concurrent control group.
strengths: Diverse international sites, large absolute changes and a simple, transferable intervention.
limitations: A before–after design cannot separate the checklist from secular trends, observation effects and the motivation of volunteer sites. Team training and attention that accompanied implementation are bundled with the tool.
contested: Ontario’s mandated, province-wide adoption found no significant reduction in mortality or complications (R-urbach-2014-introduction). The difference is usually discussed in terms of implementation, site selection and baseline risk.
generalizability: The tool travels easily; the effect appears to depend on how it is implemented. For organizations and sport, the transferable lesson concerns implementation conditions more than checklist content.
relevance: The classic evidence for checklists as decision hygiene and — read with the Ontario study — a lesson in why the same process tool can work in one setting and not another.

title: Introduction of Surgical Safety Checklists in Ontario, Canada
license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, first author, journal, volume, issue, pages, publication date (13 March 2014) and DOI matched on PubMed (PMID 24620866); design, sample size (about 200,000 procedures) and mortality rates matched in the abstract as reported by medical news summaries. Co-authors were not displayed in results and are not recorded.

summary: A population-based study of roughly 200,000 surgical procedures at virtually all hospitals providing surgery in Ontario, comparing three-month periods before and after each hospital adopted a surgical safety checklist under a provincial requirement. Operative mortality was 0.71% before and 0.65% after, a non-significant difference, and complications did not fall significantly.
arguments: Mandated adoption of surgical safety checklists across a province was not associated with significant reductions in operative mortality or complications.
Results from enthusiastic early-adopter settings may not reproduce under policy-driven rollout.
Safety gains may depend on how teams use a tool more than on the tool itself.
design: Population-based before-and-after comparison of three-month periods around each hospital’s adoption under a provincial policy.
strengths: Very large, population-wide sample that reduces volunteer-site selection and measures the effect of policy as actually implemented.
limitations: Short comparison windows and a low baseline mortality rate limit the ability to detect small changes; outcome data alone cannot show how thoroughly teams used the checklist.
contested: Contrasts with the large improvements in the WHO study (R-haynes-2009-surgical); interpretations emphasize mandated versus engaged adoption, differences in baseline risk and the limits of before–after designs on both sides.
generalizability: Highly relevant to any organization that scales a process tool by mandate after a successful pilot, including sport organizations rolling out protocols across affiliates.
relevance: The counterweight to the checklist success story: a direct lesson in external validity and implementation for anyone who will turn a pilot into an organization-wide policy.

title: Social Structure and Organizations
publication: In James G. March (Ed.), Handbook of Organizations (pp. 142–193). Chicago: Rand McNally
license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Author, chapter title, editor, book title, publisher, year and pages (142–193) matched in several citing sources, including a Wharton-hosted article on the liability of newness and a Duke repository paper; the 1965 Rand McNally Handbook matched in university library catalogs (libcat.scu.edu, Université de Nantes). Citing sources locate the liability-of-newness argument at pp. 148–150. The URL is a library catalog record for the Handbook.

summary: Stinchcombe examines how a society’s social structure shapes the organizations founded in it. His best-known argument, the liability of newness, holds that a higher proportion of new organizations fail than old ones because they must invent and teach new roles, bear the costs of building routines, depend on cooperation among strangers and win clients away from established relationships.
arguments: New organizations must create roles and teach them to people who have not performed them.
Inventing roles and routines is costly in time, conflict and inefficiency.
New organizations depend on trust among strangers, which is thin.
They lack stable ties to the people they serve, who can stay with established providers.
design: Theoretical essay drawing on historical and sociological evidence.
strengths: Specifies mechanisms rather than only a correlation between age and failure, and launched decades of empirical research on organizational founding and mortality.
limitations: The mechanisms are argued rather than measured, and the claim concerns whole organizations rather than units inside them.
contested: Later work on organizational mortality found that failure risk does not always decline from founding; some populations show low early risk followed by a peak (the liability of adolescence; R-bruderl-1990-organizational).
generalizability: Transfers by analogy to new departments and functions inside organizations, where “death” takes the form of merger, starvation or neglect. That transfer is an inference, not a tested result.
relevance: The foundational account of why a newly created function is fragile for structural reasons — essential background for designing the capstone department’s first year.

title: Organizational Mortality: The Liabilities of Newness and Adolescence
license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume, issue, pages and year matched on the University of Mannheim repository (madoc.bib.uni-mannheim.de) and citing reference lists; the DOI matched in a citing review and corresponds to the JSTOR stable identifier 2393316. The abstract and data were not available in results; the description below relies on how citing work characterizes the paper.

summary: Brüderl and Schüssler contrast two accounts of how organizational failure risk changes with age: the liability of newness, in which risk is highest at founding and declines, and a liability of adolescence, in which risk is low at first — a “honeymoon” sustained by initial resources and commitments — then rises before it declines.
arguments: Failure risk may rise during an organization’s early period before falling, rather than falling from founding.
An initial endowment of resources and commitments can protect a new organization for a time.
The two accounts differ mainly in what they predict for the period shortly after founding.
design: Empirical analysis of organizational failure rates by age; sample details were not confirmed in search results and are not described here.
strengths: Clarifies that “new organizations are risky” can describe different curve shapes, which changes when risk peaks.
limitations: Concerns whole organizations rather than internal units; this record’s description relies on citing sources rather than the full text.
contested: Part of a long debate over the shape of age dependence in organizational mortality (newness versus adolescence and other patterns); see R-stinchcombe-1965-social.
generalizability: For internal units, it suggests that a sponsor’s initial budget and goodwill act as an endowment, and that the dangerous period may arrive when that endowment runs out. This is an analogy, not a tested result.
relevance: Shifts the question for a new department from “how do we survive launch?” to “what must be true before the honeymoon ends?” — a timing insight for any first-year plan.

title: The First 90 Days: Proven Strategies for Getting Up to Speed Faster and Smarter
publication: Harvard Business Review Press, Boston (updated and expanded edition; first published 2003)
license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, subtitle, author, publisher (Harvard Business Review Press), publication date (14 May 2013), ISBN 9781422188613 and description as the updated, expanded tenth-anniversary edition matched on retailer and public-library catalog listings; chapter topics (prepare yourself, accelerate your learning, match strategy to situation, negotiate success) matched in a library record; IMD’s page for the book appeared in results.

summary: A practitioner guide to leadership transitions. Watkins organizes the first months in a new role around tasks such as preparing yourself, accelerating your learning, matching strategy to the situation, negotiating success with your boss and securing early wins, and offers a typology of situations — start-up, turnaround, accelerated growth, realignment and sustaining success — that changes what a leader should do first.
arguments: Transitions fail when leaders misdiagnose the situation they have inherited or misread their boss’s expectations.
What to do first depends on whether the unit is a start-up, a turnaround, in accelerated growth, in need of realignment or sustaining success.
Early wins build credibility and momentum if they serve the longer-term agenda.
design: Practitioner synthesis based on the author’s teaching, consulting and work with leaders in transition; not a controlled study.
strengths: Concrete, well-organized sequencing; the situational typology guards against one-size-fits-all advice.
limitations: Prescriptions have not been tested against comparison groups; success stories dominate; “ninety days” is a planning convention rather than an empirically derived window.
contested: No replication literature exists for its prescriptions; treat them as practitioner heuristics.
generalizability: Used across industries and the public sector; transfers to new roles in sport organizations as a sequencing aid rather than as evidence.
relevance: The most widely used practitioner playbook for a leader’s first months, read here beside the research on new organizations so you can see where the two agree and where the book outruns the evidence.

title: Performing a Project Premortem
license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, author, venue, volume, issue, pages (18–19), September 2007 issue and the hbr.org URL matched in search results, including the Wikipedia pre-mortem entry and reprint listings; the entry also links the method to earlier prospective-hindsight research by Mitchell, Russo and Pennington (1989).

summary: A two-page description of the premortem. Before a project is finalized, the team imagines that it has already failed and each member independently writes plausible reasons. Klein argues that the technique surfaces problems early, reduces overconfidence, sensitizes the team to early signs of trouble and makes dissent a legitimate assignment rather than disloyalty.
arguments: Assuming failure as a fact makes it easier to generate reasons for it than asking what might go wrong.
The method gives people who doubt a plan a legitimate way to say so.
The risks surfaced should change the plan, not merely be recorded.
design: Practitioner article describing a technique; it draws on earlier laboratory research on prospective hindsight rather than reporting a new study.
strengths: Cheap, fast and easy to run; turns raising risks into an assigned task.
limitations: No controlled organizational trials are reported; results depend on the diversity of the team; it can produce long, unprioritized lists.
contested: The size of the benefit in organizations has not been established experimentally.
generalizability: Applies to any project or decision review, from product launches to department plans and season preparation.
relevance: A concrete tool for stress-testing the capstone recommendation before a skeptical president or owner does.

title: The Artful Dodger: Answering the Wrong Question the Right Way
license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume, issue, pages and year matched on a PubMed-indexed listing (PMID 21517203), the American Psychological Association press release (EurekAlert) and Harvard Magazine; an author-hosted PDF appeared on toddrogers.scholars.harvard.edu. One result gave a DOI, but a second search could not confirm it, so no DOI is recorded.

summary: In four studies using recorded debate answers, listeners often failed to notice when a speaker answered a similar but different question, and rated that speaker as trustworthy and likable as one who answered directly. Clearly different answers were penalized, and so were halting answers to the right question. Displaying the question while the speaker answered made dodges far easier to detect.
arguments: Answers to a similar question frequently go undetected as dodges.
Fluent delivery is rewarded even when the content dodges; a smooth dodger can be preferred to a stammering answerer.
Keeping the original question salient sharply increases detection — in the press summary, from 39% to 88% of listeners.
design: Four experiments in which participants evaluated debate answers that addressed the question asked, a similar question or a clearly different question.
strengths: Controlled manipulations separate the content of an answer from its delivery.
limitations: Participants had no relationship with the speaker and no stake in the decision; the setting is political debate; how often dodges succeed in boardrooms is unknown.
generalizability: The mechanism plausibly transfers to executive settings; the magnitudes do not. Boards that read pre-reads, know the speaker and repeat their questions may catch dodges more often.
relevance: Shows why direct answers to hard questions are a matter of integrity and governance, not style — and how a skilled questioner keeps a dodge from working.

title: Outcome Bias in Decision Evaluation
publication: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 54(4), 569–579
license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume, issue, pages and year matched on a scanned copy hosted by the University of Florida, the Wikipedia outcome-bias entry and a PubMed Central replication article; a search on the DOI returned this article.

summary: In five studies, undergraduates evaluated decisions made under uncertainty — medical decisions and monetary gambles — after being told how they turned out. Decisions with favorable outcomes were rated as better reasoned and their makers as more competent, although the information available at the time was the same. Participants who said outcomes should not matter were still influenced by them.
arguments: People judge the quality of a decision partly by its outcome, even when the outcome could not have been known.
Outcome information also changes judgments of the decision-maker’s competence.
Knowing that outcomes should not matter does not prevent the bias.
design: Five experiments in which undergraduate participants rated hypothetical decisions whose outcomes were varied.
strengths: Clean manipulation of outcome with the decision held constant; a simple, influential paradigm.
limitations: Student participants and written vignettes; the size of the effect in organizations with real stakes and richer information is not established by these studies.
contested: Not contested in direction. A later pre-registered replication of Experiment 1 (“Outcomes Affect Evaluations of Decision Quality: Replication and Extensions of Baron and Hershey’s (1988) Outcome Bias Experiment 1”, indexed in PubMed Central) reproduced the effect.
generalizability: Strong reason to expect the bias in organizational reviews, where outcomes are known before decisions are evaluated; do not assume the vignette magnitudes.
relevance: The research basis for judging process separately from results — the core of every after-action review and personal decision journal.

title: Do Team and Individual Debriefs Enhance Performance? A Meta-Analysis
license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume, issue, pages, year (online June 2012) and DOI matched on PubMed (PMID 23516804) and journals.sagepub.com; the main result (46 samples, N = 2,136, about 25%, d = .67) and moderators matched the abstract; a full-text copy appeared on cebma.org (Center for Evidence-Based Management).

summary: A meta-analysis of 46 samples (N = 2,136) of team and individual debriefs drawn from published and unpublished research. On average, debriefs improved performance over control conditions by approximately 25% (d = 0.67). Effects were stronger when debriefs were aligned with objectives, and facilitation and structure appeared to contribute.
arguments: Debriefs improve individual and team performance on average by a practically meaningful amount.
Alignment between the debrief and specific objectives strengthens the effect.
Facilitation and structure may increase benefits.
A debrief must meet a defined set of essential elements; loosely run reviews are not what the estimate describes.
design: Meta-analysis of published and unpublished studies of interventions that met the authors’ definition of a debrief.
strengths: Pools many studies across team and individual settings; tests moderators; includes unpublished work.
limitations: Included studies vary in setting and design; moderator findings rest on fewer studies; an average effect does not tell any single organization what to expect.
generalizability: Supports structured reviews in organizations and sport, with the caveat that implementation quality varies and field settings with long feedback delays are less directly represented.
relevance: The strongest single summary of whether after-action reviews and debriefs work, and of the design features that matter.

title: A Leader’s Guide to After-Action Reviews (Training Circular 25-20)
publication: U.S. Department of the Army, Washington, DC (30 September 1993)
license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, issuing body (Headquarters, Department of the Army), series number (TC 25-20) and date (30 September 1993) matched in a Taiwan Ministry of National Defense document and in citations within a U.S. Army Research Institute report on dtic.mil; gurteen.com describes it as a leader’s guide to planning, preparing and conducting AARs that supplements FM 25-101. No official copy of the circular appeared in results; one source reports it was later replaced by a 2011 Combined Arms Center guide. The URL is a description page, not the circular.

summary: The U.S. Army’s guide to planning, preparing and conducting after-action reviews: professional discussions of an event, focused on performance standards, that help participants discover for themselves what happened, why it happened and how to sustain strengths and improve on weaknesses. It covers reviews ranging from formal, facilitated sessions to informal discussions held on the spot.
arguments: A review should compare what was supposed to happen with what actually happened, and explain the difference.
Participants should discover lessons themselves rather than receive a critique.
Reviews range from formal to informal and should follow events closely.
design: Training doctrine and procedural guidance, not a study.
strengths: A detailed, field-tested procedure from an organization that built the practice into routine training.
limitations: Doctrine is not evidence of effectiveness; written for military training contexts; later superseded by newer Army guidance.
generalizability: Widely adapted in firefighting, healthcare and business. Evidence that such reviews improve performance comes from debrief research such as R-tannenbaum-2013-do, not from the guide itself.
relevance: The institutional model for after-action reviews, useful as a template for the reviews you will run on your own decisions and your department’s.
